patient.chief_complaint: Partner called 911 after patient developed sudden worst headache of life while watching sports, now vomiting
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Parker is a 53-year-old man with hypertension, bipolar disorder on lithium, and active tobacco use who is brought in by ambulance after his partner called 911. He was watching a sports game on TV when he suddenly screamed and grabbed his head. He describes the headache as the worst pain of his life, instantaneous onset, rated 10/10. He vomited twice and had transient confusion that resolved. He is now fully alert. He has marked neck stiffness and photophobia. He has no prior history of severe headaches. His medications include lithium carbonate 600 mg twice daily for bipolar disorder and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg for hypertension. The lithium is a significant concern in the context of SAH for two reasons: first, lithium has a narrow therapeutic window and SAH-associated hyponatremia and fluid shifts can cause lithium toxicity; second, the thiazide diuretic is already known to increase lithium levels. Additionally, HCTZ creates hypovolemia risk during SAH — a critical concern since hypovolemia worsens DCI. Furthermore, many SAH patients develop cerebral salt wasting with hyponatremia, and lithium monitoring becomes essential as sodium fluctuates. His BP is severely elevated on arrival. The smoking history is a major modifiable risk factor.

output.summary: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage frequently causes hyponatremia through cerebral salt wasting or SIADH. Hyponatremia reduces renal lithium clearance, raising serum lithium concentrations toward the toxic range. Published case series and pharmacokinetic data support monitoring lithium levels at least every 24–48 hours in patients on lithium who develop SAH, with more frequent sampling if sodium falls. Lithium toxicity (coarse tremor, nystagmus, ataxia, confusion) may be clinically difficult to distinguish from delayed cerebral ischemia. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: CSW is more common cause of hyponatremia in SAH than SIADH
CSW: hypovolemia + high urine sodium - treat with IV normal saline or hypertonic saline
SIADH: euvolemia + low urine osmolality - fluid restrict cautiously (risky in SAH due to DCI)
In SAH, maintain euvolemia; excessive fluid restriction risks DCI
Lithium toxicity watch: if Na drops, lithium levels increase - check both together

output.summary: Hyponatremia in aneurysmal SAH occurs most commonly through cerebral salt wasting, characterized by hypovolemia and urinary sodium wasting; SIADH is the next most common mechanism and is distinguished by euvolemia and inappropriately concentrated urine. Differentiation is clinically important because management differs: CSW is treated with isotonic or hypertonic saline replacement, while SIADH management in SAH requires caution given the risk of hypovolemia-induced delayed cerebral ischemia. Euvolemia is a recognized goal of care in the vasospasm window regardless of the mechanism of hyponatremia. Clinical correlation recommended.
